claims.text: RHEAs derive superior high-temperature mechanical behavior from high configurational entropy.
RHEAs derive superior high-temperature thermoelastic behavior from high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy induces significant local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
Local lattice distortions favor a stable, reversible elastic response during high-temperature fluctuations.
High-temperature homogenization annealing ensures chemical uniformity after arc melting.
Removing one or more alloying elements lowers configurational entropy.
Multiple principal elements create a broad distribution of atomic sizes and bonding strengths.
Heterogeneous atomic sizes and bonding strengths produce local lattice distortions.
Distortion-induced barriers to dislocation motion enhance yield strength.
Reducing configurational entropy decreases local lattice distortions and their beneficial mechanical and thermoelastic effects.
At 1200°C, the full high-entropy alloy will have higher yield strength than the lower-entropy variant.
Under cyclic high-temperature conditions, the full high-entropy alloy will exhibit a more stable and reversible thermoelastic strain response than the lower-entropy variant.
The high-entropy sample will exhibit greater diffraction peak broadening than the lower-entropy sample.
Greater X-ray diffraction peak broadening is an indicator of greater local lattice distortion.
The proposed mechanism is applicable only while the alloy remains single-phase BCC and oxidation, multiphase formation, and grain-boundary-dominated behavior are absent or negligible.

contradictions.description: The intervention and baseline define entropy reduction by removing one or more minor elements, whereas the falsification design describes reducing the number of principal elements. These are materially different compositional interventions and may produce different entropy changes and confounders.
